cards.q: What is the difference between raylib and a game engine?
cards.a:
raylib is a library of functions you call from your own loop; an engine gives you an editor and systems your game fits into

raylib has no editor or scene tree: you write the loop and call its functions. It also draws 3D, so the 2D-only answer is wrong.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: What does `vcpkg integrate install` do?
cards.a:
It makes Visual Studio projects find the headers and libraries vcpkg installed, with no project settings

Integration is a one-time step that hooks vcpkg into every Visual Studio project. Installing raylib itself is the separate `vcpkg install raylib:x64-windows` command.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: When does `WindowShouldClose()` become true?
cards.a:
When the user presses Esc or clicks the window's close button

It reports the user's request to quit; your loop then ends and you call `CloseWindow()` yourself.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: Why does the practice on this site check game logic instead of drawing a window?
cards.a:
Because Compiler Explorer has no window or GPU to draw on

Only the logic around raylib's calls can run there, so the practice declares the raylib types it needs and tests that logic, which moves into a real raylib project unchanged. raylib works fine from C++.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: What are the three steps of every frame?
cards.a:
Read input, update the world, draw the world

Each frame reads input, changes the game's state a little, then draws it as it is now. Loading and freeing happen once, outside the loop.

cards.q: What happens if you do not call `ClearBackground` at the start of a frame?
cards.a:
The new frame is drawn over an old one, so moving objects leave trails

The back buffer still holds an older frame. Without clearing, everything drawn earlier stays visible underneath.

cards.q: Where does raylib read the keyboard and mouse for the next frame?
cards.a:
In `EndDrawing`, after showing the frame

`EndDrawing` swaps buffers, waits for the target frame rate and polls input, so `IsKeyPressed` reports what happened since the previous frame.

cards.q: Why does the lesson's `draw` function take the game as `const Game&`?
cards.a:
So drawing can read the game state but cannot change it

`const&` gives read-only access without a copy. Keeping state changes in `update` lets you pause, speed up or test the update without a window.

cards.q: Which way does y grow in raylib's screen coordinates?
cards.a:
Downwards: the top of the window is y = 0

Screen y points down, so moving "up" subtracts from y and gravity adds to it, unlike a maths graph.

cards.q: What does the position of a rectangle and of a circle refer to?
cards.a:
A rectangle by its top-left corner, a circle by its centre

Mixing the two up is the most common reason a shape ends up half its size off.

cards.q: How do you centre text horizontally?
cards.a:
Start it at (screen width - `MeasureText` width) / 2

Measure the text with `MeasureText` and subtract its width. Starting at half the screen width puts the text's left edge in the middle, and the font size is the height, not the width.

cards.q: What alpha value makes a colour fully solid?
cards.a:
255

`Color` stores each channel as an `unsigned char` from 0 to 255: 255 is solid and 0 is invisible. `Fade` takes a 0-1 float, but the stored alpha is 0-255.

cards.q: Why multiply speeds by `GetFrameTime()`?
cards.a:
So movement is measured per second and is the same at every frame rate

dt is the length of the last frame, so speed × dt moves the same distance each second whatever the frame rate. Capping the frame rate is what `SetTargetFPS` does.

cards.q: Why is diagonal movement too fast without normalising the direction?
cards.a:
The direction (1, 1) has length about 1.41, so the speed is about 41 % higher

Each axis gets the full speed, and the combined vector is √2 long. Normalising it to length 1 before scaling fixes that.

cards.q: Why clamp dt to a maximum such as 0.05 s?
cards.a:
So one very long frame cannot move objects through walls

A long frame (a dragged window, a debugger pause) would make one huge step that skips through walls. Clamping makes the game slow down briefly instead of breaking.

cards.q: A shot cooldown is reset with `cooldown += 0.25f` rather than `cooldown = 0.25f`. Why?
cards.a:
Adding it back keeps the average firing rate exact

Frames rarely divide the period evenly; with `+=` the time overshot past zero is carried into the next period instead of being lost each shot.

cards.q: Why is `vel *= pow(0.1f, dt)` better for friction than `vel *= 0.9f` each frame?
cards.a:
It keeps 10 % of the speed per second at any frame rate

A fixed factor per frame depends on the frame rate: at 120 FPS a per-frame 0.9 is applied twice as often as at 60 FPS. Raising the factor to the power dt makes it a per-second rule.

cards.q: When do you use `IsKeyDown` and when `IsKeyPressed`?
cards.a:
`IsKeyDown` for moving, `IsKeyPressed` for jumping

Down is for actions that continue while held; Pressed is true once per press, for one-off actions such as a jump or a menu choice. Using Down for a menu moves the selection every frame the key is held.

cards.q: Why read typed text with `GetCharPressed` instead of key codes?
cards.a:
It returns real characters for the user's keyboard layout and Shift state

Key codes name positions on a US keyboard. `GetCharPressed` gives the Unicode characters actually typed, one by one in a loop.

cards.q: What is a dead zone on a gamepad stick?
cards.a:
A small range around the stick's centre that is read as zero

A stick at rest reads a few hundredths, not 0, so without a dead zone drift moves the character. The dead zone ignores that and rescales the rest so movement still starts smoothly.

cards.q: Why map actions such as `Action::Jump` to keys instead of testing `KEY_SPACE` in the game code?
cards.a:
So the bindings can be changed without changing the game code

The game asks "did the player jump?" and a binding list answers it from any key or gamepad button, which is what a rebinding screen edits.

cards.q: What is the difference between an `Image` and a `Texture2D`?
cards.a:
An `Image` is pixels in main memory for editing; a `Texture2D` lives in video memory and is what you draw

Edit or generate pixels in an `Image` on the CPU; draw from a `Texture2D` on the GPU.

cards.q: Why must textures be loaded after `InitWindow`?
cards.a:
Because creating a texture needs the OpenGL context that `InitWindow` creates

No context, no video memory to put the texture in. For the same reason `UnloadTexture` must come before `CloseWindow`.

cards.q: How do you draw a sprite facing the other way without a second picture?
cards.a:
Give the source rectangle a negative width

A negative source width flips the picture horizontally. Rotating by 180 would turn it upside down as well.

cards.q: Small pixel-art sprites look blurry when scaled up. What fixes it?
cards.a:
`SetTextureFilter(tex, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT)` and scaling by whole numbers

The default bilinear filtering blends neighbouring pixels. Point filtering keeps them crisp, and whole-number scales make every source pixel the same size.

cards.q: What does `DrawTexturePro`'s `origin` do?
cards.a:
It is the pivot point, measured from `dest`'s top-left corner

`dest.x, dest.y` is where the pivot lands on screen, and rotation turns around it. Put the origin at the centre of `dest` and the sprite spins around its middle. The part of the texture is the `source` rectangle.

cards.q: Why should animation time be measured in seconds, not game frames?
cards.a:
So the animation plays at the same speed whatever the frame rate

Counting game frames would make the walk cycle twice as fast at 120 FPS as at 60, just like moving by pixels per frame.

cards.q: Why must `play()` not restart an animation that is already playing?
cards.a:
It is called every frame, so restarting each time would keep the animation on its first frame

`play(walk)` runs every frame while walking. Only a change of animation should reset the time to 0.

cards.q: What is the difference between a looping and a one-shot animation?
cards.a:
A looping animation wraps back to its first frame; a one-shot stops on its last frame and reports that it has finished

Idle and walk loop with `%`; attack, hurt and death stop on their last frame, and `finished()` tells the game to move on.

cards.q: In a sheet with 8 frames per row, which source rectangle holds frame 10 if each frame is 32 × 32?
cards.a:
`{ 64, 32, 32, 32 }`

Column `10 % 8 = 2` gives x = 64, row `10 / 8 = 1` gives y = 32. `{ 320, 0, 32, 32 }` forgets the rows, and `{ 32, 64, ... }` swaps column and row.

cards.q: A footstep sound should play on frame 1 of the walk. When do you play it?
cards.a:
When the frame number changes to 1

The frame stays at 1 for several game frames; checking while it *is* 1 would play the sound repeatedly.

cards.q: Why should you not keep the pointer `TextFormat` returns?
cards.a:
It points to a buffer inside raylib that later calls reuse

raylib keeps only a few buffers, so a stored pointer soon holds some other text. Use the result straight away, or copy it into a `std::string`.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: How do you right-align a score at x = 780?
cards.a:
Measure the text and draw it at 780 - width

`x - width / 2` would centre it on 780. Right-aligned digits do not shift when the number gets longer.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: Why is the interface drawn outside the camera?
cards.a:
So it stays fixed on the screen while the world moves under it

The interface is drawn after the world, in screen coordinates; inside the camera it would scroll away with the world.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: Why load a font with `LoadFontEx` at the size you will draw it?
cards.a:
Because the glyphs are stored as pictures at that one size

A font is an atlas of glyph pictures: drawing much bigger looks blurry and much smaller looks grainy, so load each size you use a lot.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: When do you use `Sound` and when `Music`?
cards.a:
`Sound` for short effects loaded fully into memory; `Music` for long tracks streamed from the file

Both types read WAV and OGG; the difference is how they are loaded. A fully loaded `Sound` starts instantly, while streamed `Music` uses little memory.

cards.q: What happens if you forget to call `UpdateMusicStream` every frame?
cards.a:
The stream's buffer is not refilled, so the music stops almost straight away

`UpdateMusicStream` refills the buffer from the file. Without it you hear a fraction of a second, the most common raylib audio bug.

cards.q: Why use sound aliases made with `LoadSoundAlias`?
cards.a:
Because playing a `Sound` that is already playing restarts it; aliases let several copies play at once

Aliases share the sample data, so a few of them played in turn let rapid coins or gunshots overlap instead of cutting each other off.

cards.q: Why map a volume slider through decibels instead of straight to amplitude?
cards.a:
Because loudness is heard roughly logarithmically

A straight mapping seems to do nothing for most of its range: halving the amplitude is only about -6 dB. Spreading the slider over -40 to 0 dB makes each step sound like a similar change.

cards.q: What makes a game's set of screens a state machine?
cards.a:
There is exactly one current screen, and events switch it

States, one current state, and transitions triggered by events. An enum and two switches is already a state machine; classes are just one way to write it.

cards.q: Why is a stack of scenes useful for a pause menu?
cards.a:
The game stays below the menu, frozen and still drawn, and popping the menu returns to it exactly as it was

Only the top scene is updated, so the game is frozen; the pause menu does not cover what is below, so the game is still drawn behind it.

cards.q: Why should scenes request stack changes instead of changing the stack directly?
cards.a:
Because popping the running scene would destroy it mid-update

Popping the scene whose `update` is running destroys it while its code is still executing. The stack applies the requested push, pop or replace after the update, when no scene's code is running.

cards.q: How should "Play again" reset the game?
cards.a:
Keep a play-through's state in one struct and assign a fresh one: `game = Game{};`

Leftover timers, enemies or particles from the last round are a common bug; assigning a new struct resets everything at once.

cards.q: What is an AABB?
cards.a:
An axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the x and y axes

Because it is never rotated, testing two AABBs takes only a few comparisons. Rotating objects are usually given circles instead.

cards.q: Why compare squared distances when testing two circles?
cards.a:
It gives the same answer as comparing distances, without the cost of a square root

Both sides are non-negative, so `dx² + dy² < (ra + rb)²` holds exactly when the distance is less than the sum of the radii.

cards.q: How do you test a circle against a rectangle?
cards.a:
Clamp the circle's centre to the rectangle to find the closest point, and check whether that point is within the radius

The bounding-square shortcut wrongly counts hits near the rectangle's corners, and the centre-only test misses a circle that overlaps an edge.

cards.q: Why does the rectangle test use `<` rather than `<=`?
cards.a:
So rectangles that only touch do not count as overlapping

With `<=`, a right edge exactly at another's left edge would be an overlap, and a character standing on a floor tile would always be "inside" it.

cards.q: Along which axis do you push an overlapping rectangle out?
cards.a:
The one where the overlap is smaller: the shortest way out

Pushing out along the smaller overlap moves the object the least distance; this is the minimum translation vector.

cards.q: Why move and resolve one axis at a time?
cards.a:
Each move's direction then tells you which side was hit

After a horizontal-only move, a hit must be on the left or right side. Characters then slide along walls, do not catch on tile seams, and get `onGround` for free when a downward move is blocked.

cards.q: What is tunnelling?
cards.a:
A fast object skipping past a thin wall between two frames

No overlap is ever detected: a bullet moving 20 pixels a frame can skip over an 8-pixel wall. Clamping dt, sub-steps or sweeping the path fixes it.

cards.q: With a floor normal `n = (0, -1)`, which formula makes a ball bounce off the floor?
cards.a:
`v -= 2 * dot(v, n) * n`

Removing the normal part once makes the ball slide; removing it twice reflects it, and adding it pushes the ball faster into the floor. Multiply by a bounciness below 1 so each bounce loses energy.

cards.q: How do you get gravity and jump speed from a jump height h and a rise time t?
cards.a:
gravity = 2h / t², jump speed = 2h / t

A 96-pixel jump rising in 0.4 s needs gravity 1200 px/s² and jump speed 480 px/s. The factor 2 comes from starting fast and slowing to zero.

cards.q: What is coyote time?
cards.a:
A short time after walking off a ledge during which the player can still jump

About 0.1 s of grace, because the player saw themselves on the ledge. Remembering a press made just before landing is jump buffering.

cards.q: Why clear both the coyote and buffer timers when the jump happens?
cards.a:
Otherwise the same press or the same ledge can trigger a second jump

Either timer still running after the jump could make one press, or one ledge, count again a frame later.

cards.q: How is variable jump height usually done?
cards.a:
By cutting the upward speed (for example halving it) when the button is released while still rising

The jump starts at full speed on the press; letting go early cuts it short, so a tap is a small hop.

cards.q: What does the accumulator hold after the step loop?
cards.a:
Leftover real time not yet simulated, under one step

Each frame adds the frame time and every step removes `step`; what remains (less than one step) is carried over to the next frame.

cards.q: What is the spiral of death, and how do you avoid it?
cards.a:
Steps take longer to compute than they simulate, so frames keep slowing; cap the steps

Each slow frame owes more steps, which makes the next frame slower still. Limiting the steps per frame (or clamping the frame time) lets the game slow down instead of freezing completely.

cards.q: What is `alpha` in interpolation?
cards.a:
`accumulator / step`, how far between the last two steps

It runs from 0 to 1. Drawing `prev + (curr - prev) * alpha` gives every frame a slightly different position, so motion is smooth on high-refresh screens.

cards.q: A frame runs zero fixed steps, and in it the player pressed jump. What should happen?
cards.a:
The press is stored in a flag that the next step consumes

Input is read once per frame but used by the steps; a flag consumed by the first step means the press is neither lost in a zero-step frame nor used twice in a two-step frame.

cards.q: What are the broad phase and the narrow phase?
cards.a:
The broad phase cheaply finds pairs that might collide; the narrow phase runs the exact test on those pairs only

A grid is a broad phase: it rules out pairs on opposite sides of the world so the real circle or rectangle test runs on few pairs.

cards.q: Why is an object inserted into every grid cell it touches?
cards.a:
So objects across a cell boundary still share a cell

If an object were only in the cell of its centre, a neighbour just across the boundary would never meet it and the pair would not be tested.

cards.q: How do you avoid testing the same pair twice when two objects share several cells?
cards.a:
Remember tested pairs (a < b), or test each pair in one agreed cell

The agreed cell can be the one containing the top-left corner of the pair's overlap. Inserting into one cell only would miss pairs across boundaries.

cards.q: Roughly how big should a grid cell be?
cards.a:
About twice the size of a typical object, then adjusted after measuring

Too small and big objects fill many cells; too large and each cell holds many objects, back towards n squared.

cards.q: What do a Camera2D's `target` and `offset` mean?
cards.a:
`target` is the world point the camera looks at; `offset` is where on the screen that point is drawn

The target is in world coordinates and the offset in screen coordinates: a world point `p` appears at `(p - target) * zoom + offset`, so an offset at the screen's centre keeps the target in the middle.

cards.q: How do you find which world point the mouse is over?
cards.a:
`GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), camera)`

The mouse is in screen coordinates, so convert screen to world. `GetWorldToScreen2D` goes the other way, and simply adding the target ignores the offset and zoom.

cards.q: What is a camera dead zone?
cards.a:
A box around the screen's centre within which the player can move without the camera moving

While the player stays inside the box the camera stays still; it moves only enough to keep the player in the box, so small movements do not shake the view.

cards.q: Why store a tile map as one flat vector?
cards.a:
It is a single block of memory indexed with `y * width + x`, which is fast and simple

One contiguous block with one index formula is faster and simpler than a vector of vectors, where each row is a separate allocation.

cards.q: What happens to object letters such as P or E when loading a level?
cards.a:
Their positions are recorded in object lists, and the map gets an empty tile there

Objects are not tiles: the loader records the player start, enemy spawns and coins in lists and leaves an empty tile in the grid.

cards.q: How does 4-neighbour auto-tiling choose a tile?
cards.a:
It builds a 4-bit number from which neighbours are solid and uses it to pick one of 16 pictures

One bit per side (above, right, below, left) gives 0 to 15. A plain count would mix up different shapes, such as a column (above and below) and a corner (above and right).

cards.q: Why use a fixed pool for particles?
cards.a:
It avoids allocating and freeing memory for hundreds of short-lived objects every second

With a fixed capacity and a living count, nothing is allocated after start-up and the update walks one tight array, instead of `new`/`delete` or `push_back`/`erase` hundreds of times a second.

cards.q: How does "swap and pop" remove particle `i`?
cards.a:
Copy the last living particle into slot `i` and reduce the living count by one

The living particles stay packed at the front without shifting the rest. It changes their order, which does not matter for particles.

cards.q: When do you use additive blending?
cards.a:
For things that emit light, such as fire, sparks and magic, so overlaps glow brighter

Additive blending adds colours, so overlapping sparks get brighter. Smoke and dust use normal alpha blending, which covers and darkens instead.

cards.q: Why should every state change go through one `enter` function?
cards.a:
So the timer is always reset and the state's start actions always run, from wherever the change comes

One place where a state starts means its timer is always reset and its enter actions (such as starting the attack animation) always run, even for changes from outside like being hit.

cards.q: How do you test whether the player is in an enemy's field of view?
cards.a:
Compare the dot product of the facing direction and the direction to the player with the cosine of half the view angle

With both directions normalised, `dot(f, d)` is the cosine of the angle between them, so the player is in view when `dot(f, d) > cos(halfAngle)`. Comparing it with the angle itself mixes a cosine with an angle.

cards.q: What is telegraphing?
cards.a:
Showing an attack is coming, such as a wind-up animation, so the player has time to react

A visible wind-up makes attacks fair and readable. The pause after spotting the player is the reaction time, a related but different idea.

cards.q: Why does BFS find a shortest path when all steps cost the same?
cards.a:
It reaches tiles in order of their distance from the start

BFS spreads like a ripple: all tiles at distance 1, then 2, and so on, so the first time it reaches the goal is by a shortest path. It does not aim at the goal at all; that is what A* adds.

cards.q: What are g, h and f in A*?
cards.a:
g is the cost so far, h is the estimated remaining cost, and f = g + h; A* expands the smallest f first

A* picks the tile with the smallest estimated total `f = g + h` from a priority queue. Expanding by `h` alone ignores the cost already paid and can miss the shortest path.

cards.q: When is a flow field better than many path searches?
cards.a:
When many units head for the same target: one search from the target serves all of them

One BFS or Dijkstra from the target stores every tile's distance, and each unit steps to its neighbour with the smallest one, so the cost no longer grows with the number of units. A* handles terrain costs fine by adding them to `g`.

cards.q: Which way does y point in raylib's 3D space?
cards.a:
Up

raylib's 3D space is right-handed and y-up: x right, y up, z towards the viewer. Only 2D screen coordinates have y pointing down.

cards.q: What is the difference between perspective and orthographic projection?
cards.a:
Perspective makes distant things smaller; orthographic keeps sizes the same at every distance

Perspective works like a real eye. Orthographic keeps sizes constant, which suits strategy and isometric games, and then `fovy` is the height of the view in world units rather than being ignored.

cards.q: What does the dot product of two normalised directions tell you?
cards.a:
The cosine of the angle between them

`a · b = |a||b| cos θ`, so for unit vectors it is `cos θ`: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular, -1 for opposite. The perpendicular vector is what the cross product gives.

cards.q: Why is the pitch clamped to about ±89°?
cards.a:
So the camera never looks straight up or down past the vertical, where the view would flip

Past the vertical, the view flips over the top. Turning around is yaw, which is not clamped, and `std::sin` works for any angle.

cards.q: Why walk with the flat forward direction instead of the full look direction?
cards.a:
So looking up or down does not change walking speed

The flat forward direction uses the yaw only, with y = 0. With the full look direction, looking down would point part of the movement into the ground and make you walk slower.

cards.q: How does a third-person camera find its position?
cards.a:
It starts from a point on the player and moves back along the view direction by the camera distance

The camera orbits the player: `target` is a point on the player (about the shoulders) and `position = target - offset`, where the offset is the view direction from yaw and pitch scaled by the distance. A fixed offset would not turn with the view.

cards.q: How do you find what the mouse is pointing at in 3D?
cards.a:
Turn the mouse position into a ray from the camera with `GetScreenToWorldRay`, test it against the objects and keep the nearest hit

The ray goes from the camera through the mouse position. The camera's target is only the centre of the view, and the first object in the list is not necessarily the nearest.

cards.q: In the slab method, when does the ray miss the box?
cards.a:
When the latest entry into a slab comes after the earliest exit from another (`tmin > tmax`)

The ray is inside the box only between the latest entry and the earliest exit; if those cross, there is no common stretch. A zero direction on an axis is a miss only when the start lies outside that slab.

cards.q: Why keep the hit with the smallest distance?
cards.a:
A ray can pass through several objects; the nearest one is the one actually seen or hit

Testing every object can give several hits along the same ray. The first one along it is what the player sees or the bullet hits.

cards.q: What do the vertex shader and the fragment shader do?
cards.a:
The vertex shader positions each vertex; the fragment shader chooses the colour of each pixel a triangle covers

The vertex shader runs once per vertex and places it on screen; after the rasteriser works out which pixels a triangle covers, the fragment shader runs once per pixel to choose its colour.

cards.q: What is a uniform?
cards.a:
A value set from the program that is the same for every vertex and pixel of a draw call

Uniforms are set from C++ with `SetShaderValue` after looking up their location once with `GetShaderLocation`. Per-pixel values such as `fragTexCoord` are inputs (`in`), not uniforms.

cards.q: Why does a light shader need `screenHeight - y` for the light position?
cards.a:
`gl_FragCoord` measures y from the bottom of the window, while raylib's screen coordinates measure it from the top

The two coordinate systems count y from opposite edges, so the light's y is flipped. Forgetting it puts the light upside down.

cards.q: Why is the source height negative when drawing a render texture?
cards.a:
OpenGL stores textures upside down relative to raylib's screen coordinates, so the picture must be flipped vertically

Without the negative height, the whole frame appears upside down. Filtering and scaling are set separately (texture filter and the destination rectangle).

cards.q: How do you apply a shader to the whole frame?
cards.a:
Draw the frame into a render texture, then draw that texture to the screen between `BeginShaderMode` and `EndShaderMode`

Post-processing needs the finished frame as a texture, so the fragment shader sees every pixel of it at once. Shading each object separately gives per-object effects, not a whole-frame vignette or blur.

cards.q: How do you compute a pixel's perceived brightness for grey scale?
cards.a:
`dot(colour, (0.299, 0.587, 0.114))`

The eye is most sensitive to green and least to blue, so the weights are 0.299 for red, 0.587 for green and 0.114 for blue. A plain average makes blues look too bright.

cards.q: Why draw the interface after the post-processed frame?
cards.a:
So effects such as blur, vignette or shake do not distort the text and buttons

Drawing the interface on top after the effect keeps it sharp and readable. Text can be drawn into a render texture; it would just be affected by the shader.

cards.q: Why start from defaults when loading settings?
cards.a:
Missing, damaged or new keys then keep sensible values instead of breaking the game

Overwriting defaults only with keys that are present and valid means a cut-off line or a setting added in an update simply keeps its default.

cards.q: How do you save without risking a half-written file?
cards.a:
Write to a temporary file and rename it over the old one, which replaces it in one step

A rename in the same folder is atomic, so afterwards there is either the complete old save or the complete new one. Deleting first leaves nothing at all if the game crashes during the write.

cards.q: What does a checksum protect against, and what not?
cards.a:
It detects damaged or cut-off files; it does not stop someone from editing the file on purpose

The checksum is recomputed on load and compared. Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is no protection against cheating, which is fine for a single-player game.

cards.q: Where should a Windows game write its settings and saves?
cards.a:
In the user's `%APPDATA%` folder, in a folder named after the game

A game installed in `Program Files` is not allowed to write there or next to its `.exe`, and the working directory can be anything. `%APPDATA%` is the per-user folder meant for this.

cards.q: Why does a game often show a black window when started outside Visual Studio?
cards.a:
The working directory differs, so relative asset paths break

Relative paths start from the working directory, which Visual Studio sets to the project folder. Calling `ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory())` at start-up makes them start next to the `.exe`.

cards.q: Why link the runtime statically for a release?
cards.a:
So players do not need the Visual C++ Redistributable or other DLLs installed

`/MT` (and vcpkg's `x64-windows-static` triplet) puts the runtime and raylib into the `.exe`. The large speed difference is between Debug and Release, and the console is hidden by the subsystem setting.

cards.q: What changes in the main loop for a web build?
cards.a:
The browser must call one frame function repeatedly, so the loop becomes `emscripten_set_main_loop(frame, 0, 1)`

The game has to give control back to the browser every frame, so the body of the loop moves into `frame()` and the browser calls it.

cards.q: Why describe waves as data rather than code?
cards.a:
They can be changed and rebalanced without recompiling, even while the game runs

Each line is a spawn group (time, kind, count, interval) that the spawner reads, so balancing becomes editing a text file.

cards.q: Why build the game in an order where it always runs?
cards.a:
You can test the feel at every step, and you always have a working game to show if you stop

Starting with "the toy" and adding one layer at a time keeps the game playable, so problems with the feel show up early.

cards.q: What should be in the game before you call it complete?
cards.a:
A goal, an end screen with a score, sound, and a build others can run

Also a start screen, play again and saved settings. Complete means finished, not big: one mechanic, one screen-sized world and one goal, with the screens, sound, settings and release build around it.
